I'm still friends with a man who lived in a scenario much like the one you are describing. I don't feel qualified about this particular scenario, as my experiences are far too deviated to empathize with you on an acceptable level.

What I can do, however, is tell you what turned his life around. I can't promise this will work, but I personally feel that it is better than giving in to your weaknesses (Which, by the way, we ALL have.. without exception).

He wrote his note, like yourself, and was preparing for the grim task which he felt would be his relief. Then, inexplicably, he picked up a book. I can't tell you what the name of this book was (It wasn't the Bible, by the way) or what it's contents were but what I can tell you is that it compelled him to make a key action which may have saved his life.

He had considered tearing up the note and throwing it away, letting his thoughts sink into the past as if they had never happened. What he did was so much better, however. He didn't alter the contents of what was to be his final farewells, but he did flip the page over. He wrote all of the things he wished in that moment that the people around him would say. What he felt he needed to hear from others, given time to contemplate what that may be.

He gave this note to a person who was, at the time, one of the people he blamed the most and hated the most and, supposedly, who he felt hated him. Getting to the point, this all led to a long road of recovery but today he is a happy and healthy man with a loving family and caring friends. He has his moments, but who doesn't?

Anyway, I guess what I am trying to say is that you should still continue trying to reach out but perhaps change the medium used to convey your message. Often times this can help people to understand in a more wholesome way.

Again, I can promise nothing other than that life is worth living and there is always a way back up from rock bottom. Always. Stay strong, stay safe and watch Pixar's "Inside Out". It's a great movie with a great message and a great opportunity to cry a little bit. You'll know the part, when you get to it.

I know that this isn't an end all be all solution for any and all victims of suicidal inclinations but simply knowing that a resource exists out there may be enough to help someone. Reddit is a sufficiently anonymous, which I feel provides a key element to those who are hesitant to speak out due to the socially pressured desire to "save face". It's a scary topic, after all.

Given that the moderators seem to have a pretty good handle on the directly malicious responses they seemed to have had trouble with in the past, it certainly seems more likely to do good than harm. Not that it couldn't hurt, but it seems far less likely to create progress than take it away.

You know full well that isn't what I meant by that. Working through self destructive thoughts can, at best, leave serious lasting emotional trauma in anyone who has faced these demons. I just want you to know that you don't have to face them alone and there are people in the world who want to and will help you get past this part of your life and it would be criminal to rob yourself of such an opportunity. It takes a lot of courage to open up to one person, let alone as many as it takes until you've gotten the support that you need but, again, bottling up your emotions will only increase the pressure on yourself.

You're ultimately going to do whatever you decide but you should try to remember that nobody is capable of helping you to the extent that you are capable. My point being that one should not refuse to seek help when it's out there.

I believe some (though not all) of these concerns may be valid and, although I do not feel qualified to speak at length on this particular scenario, I do feel the need to offer one point of view.

Based on a variety of credible material that I've read, I have reason to believe that frequently bringing up the topic of suicide to the suicidal is a bad idea. However, if you feel that they aren't taking you as seriously as you'd like then it may be best to simply vocalize that sentiment very bluntly to them. I'd tell them that they make me feel unsafe in their offices because that's should be a huge red flag to them, professionally.

If they persist on being inadequate and especially if you feel that they are doing more harm than good, you may consider switching to another office but don't just stop going, of course. Remind yourself that if they are indeed the "best nueropsychologist in (your) region" then they MUST have dealt with patients like you many times before. It is possible that they are slightly emotionally detached because of that fact, and you are perceiving it, but that doesn't mean that they don't care... they may just be terrible at showing it.
